title: async-kernel-queue-depth-and-sm-thresh-analysis
content:
Investigation summary

Goal:
Measure the impact of outstanding kernel queue depth (number of enqueued-but-not-completed kernels per stream) on SM-level occupancy and effective GPU utilization for our multi-stream async inference workload. Hypothesis: beyond a small in-flight kernel window, kernel enqueue congestion increases scheduling pressure and causes lower average SM occupancy and worse latency tail due to serialization and cache thrash.

Hardware / software used:
- GPU: NVIDIA A100-SXM4 80GB (single card test node)
- Driver: 535.113.01
- CUDA: 12.2
- Nsight Systems: nsys 2027.4, Nsight Compute: 2027.3
- Runtime build: serving-runtime commit 8f2b3a (experiment branch: perf/queue-depth)
- Workload: transformer decode kernels (compute-only kernels + batched KV cache management), microbatch sizes 1..8, sequence lengths 64/256

What we measured:
- Kernel enqueue interval (time between successive kernel launches from host or CPU thread)
- Outstanding kernel count per stream (measured via NVTX markers + CUPTI counters + nsys API)
- Kernel execution time distribution (per-kernel mean/std and P90)
- SM occupancy (per-kernel occupancy reported by Nsight Compute) and overall SM utilization (timeline view)
- Warp efficiency and memory issue counters (gld/gst efficiency)

Method / quick commands to reproduce:
1) Profile a baseline run (no forced queue depth):
   nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o baseline --capture-range=cudaLaunch --sample=none ./bin/runner --model tiny --microbatch 2 --seq 64
2) Instrumented run with synthetic enqueue bursts:
   ./bin/runner --microbatch 2 --burst-window 8 --burst-interval 100ms  (this forces code path that issues N kernels quickly)
3) Capture detailed kernel-level metrics with Nsight Compute for a hot kernel:
   ncu --target-processes=all --metrics sm__warps_active.avg.pct,sm__inst_executed.avg.per_cycle,pipeline_fp64_active.sum ./bin/runner
4) Use custom NVTX around kernel enqueue to count outstanding kernels (host side counter increment/decrement) and export to nsys UI.

Key observations (condensed):
- Baseline (no burst): average outstanding kernels per stream: 1.6; SM utilization steady ~93%; mean latency per token step 85us; P95 120us.
- Controlled burst (burst-window 8): outstanding kernels per stream rose to 6.8 average during bursts; SM utilization fell to 62% during sustained bursts; mean token step latency increased to 115us; P95 spiked to 320us.
- Kernel durations: hot compute kernel mean 120us, enqueue gap between kernels 30-40us under baseline; during burst the enqueue gap shrank <10us causing queue build-up in the driver's scheduling queues.
- Nsight timeline showed long sequences of serialized kernel launches on a single stream, followed by periods of SM idle. The driver appears to serialize work because multiple small kernels saturate driver enqueue and PCIe/TTI processing, and the scheduler cannot hide latency by overlap.
- Warp efficiency and memory stalls increased during bursts (gld efficiency down ~8%, memory_utilization counters spiked). We suspect increased cache thrash due to many small kernels evicting L2 lines.
- cudaGraph capture (existing e2e path) eliminated enqueue overhead and smoothed SM utilization: with cudaGraph + replay, outstanding kernel count at runtime is effectively 0 (all work recorded once), SM utilization moved back up to ~90%, mean latency 88us, P95 140us.

Microbench numbers (representative):
- Config: microbatch=2, seq=64, kernel count per step=12 (small kernels)
- Baseline: outstanding avg 1.6, SM util 93%, mean 85us, P95 120us
- Burst-window=8: outstanding avg 6.8, SM util 62%, mean 115us, P95 320us
- With cudaGraph: outstanding avg ~0 (replay), SM util 90%, mean 88us, P95 140us

Trace excerpts (human summary) from Nsight timeline:
- 00:00:00.000 host thread issues 8 launches within 85us (burst)
- 00:00:00.085 earliest kernel starts, many kernels queued behind driver internal queue
- 00:00:00.085-00:00:00.220 visible waves of kernel execution separated by idle gaps (~50-80us)
- Peak kernel serialization window corresponds to GPU queues growing >12 pending operations in driver's record.

Root causes and likely mechanisms:
1) Enqueue overhead & driver serialization: too many very short kernels cause the CUDA driver/RT to spend CPU/GPU scheduling cycles, and internal driver queues become backlogged.
2) KV cache and small per-kernel working set: many kernels touch overlapping L2 segments causing eviction and reduced locality, increasing memory stalls when kernels finally run.
3) PCIe/host-to-device signals for kernel launches (doorbell/interrupt) can become a bottleneck if launches happen in tight bursts from the host.
4) Inconsistent stream priorities: background copy streams and compute streams competed during bursts resulting in reduced async copy overlap.

Recommendations (practical mitigations):
- Short-term (engineerable quick wins):
  * Cap outstanding kernel launches at the host level with a semaphore (outstanding_limit ~= 4). This reduces tail latency spikes and keeps SM utilization higher.
  * Prefer cudaGraph capture/replay for steady-state sections of workload where the kernel sequence is stable. This removes host enqueue overhead entirely.
  * Increase per-kernel work when possible (fuse small kernels, do more work per launch). Reduces kernel count and amortizes scheduling overhead.
  * Use NVTX markers + counter to monitor outstanding kernel count in production. Add alerts when pending-kernel > 6 for >100ms.
- Mid-term (engineering and runtime):
  * Implement a persistent kernel execution pattern (persistent SM threads) for small kernels to avoid repeated launch overhead and reduce cache churn. Evaluate using cooperative groups or custom persistent loops.
  * Tune stream priorities: ensure async copies pinned to higher priority streams where beneficial; compute streams set to default high priority to preserve overlap.
  * Introduce adaptive batching in the serving runtime: when enqueue rate detected high, increase microbatch size slightly to reduce kernel count.
- Long-term / platform work:
  * Improve kernel fusion in compiler/codegen stage so we emit fewer, larger kernels for the hot path.
  * Work with drivers/partners to better understand driver queue depth limits and possible knobs (there are hints in driver logs but no public knob exposed in our driver version).

Experiments to validate mitigations planned:
- Experiment A: host-side semaphore cap at outstanding_limit=4, run 24-hour stress test with synthetic bursts, measure P95 and P99 latency and SM utilization.
- Experiment B: full cudaGraph replay path for the whole decode loop, measure end-to-end latency and memory usage across sequence lengths 32/128/512.
- Experiment C: persistent kernel prototype (micro-arch) with 1 persistent kernel handling multiple micro-ops, compare to fused-kernel approach.

Open questions / notes for follow-up:
- Does the same threshold behavior appear on Hopper/Blackwell hardware or is this A100-specific because of L2 sizing / scheduler differences? Need cross-hardware sweep.
- Driver versions: try 547.x series on a testbed to see if internal queue pressure behavior changes.
- Is the observed L2 eviction pattern reproducible in Nsight Compute mem-access analysis? We saw hints, but need a targeted L2 miss metric capture during a controlled burst.

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: implement the simple host-side semaphore cap and dashboard a metric for outstanding kernel count (1 week).
- Marco: prototype cudaGraph for the hot decode path and run set of regressions (2 weeks).
- Priya: run cross-hardware comparisons (Hopper + Blackwell nodes) and compile findings (2 weeks).

Appendix: useful commands / snippets
- Record NVTX around kernel enqueue (pseudo):
    nvtxRangePush("enqueue_kernel:x"); // increment global_atomic ++
    launch_kernel(...);
    nvtxRangePop(); // after launch increment back decrement when callback on completion
- nsys recording (capture host+cuda timeline):
    nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx -o burst-test ./bin/runner --microbatch 2 --burst-window 8
- ncu metrics for occupancy/warp efficiency:
    ncu --set full --target-processes all --metrics sm__warps_active.avg.pct,sm__pipe_tensor_cycles_active.avg.pct, l1tex__t_sectors_pipe_lsu_mem_bandwidth.avg ./bin/runner

Notes: this doc is intended as a working capture of the investigation — many traces and raw CSVs are saved in the experiment bucket and linked in the ticket JIRA-ENG-10234. The immediate pragmatic fix is host-side outstanding limit + cudaGraph where applicable; longer-term fusion/persistent kernels will require more design and benchmarks.

End of note.
